question.prompt: Jason rolls three fair standard six-sided dice. Then he looks at the rolls and chooses a subset of the dice (possibly empty, possibly all three dice) to reroll. After rerolling, he wins if and only if the sum of the numbers face up on the three dice is exactly \(7.\) Jason always plays to optimize his chances of winning. What is the probability that he chooses to reroll exactly two of the dice?

solutions.title: Compare the four reroll options
solutions.explanation:
Keeping a smaller face gives two fresh dice more ways to complete a total of \(7\). Comparing the winning probabilities for each reroll size will identify exactly which initial rolls favor rerolling two dice.

If Jason keeps a die showing \(k\) and rerolls two dice, their sum must be \(7-k\). For \(1\leq k\leq5\), the successful ordered pairs are
\[
(1,6-k),(2,5-k),\ldots,(6-k,1),
\]
so there are \(6-k\) successes among \(36\) equally likely outcomes. For \(k=6\), there are no successes. Thus the winning probability is \((6-k)/36\), and keeping the smallest die is best.

If he rerolls all three dice, first results \(1,2,3,4,5\) leave respectively \(5,4,3,2,1\) successful ordered pairs on the other dice. A first result of \(6\) cannot work. Therefore this option wins with probability
\[
\frac{5+4+3+2+1}{6^3}
=\frac{15}{216}
=\frac5{72}.
\]

Now sort the initial faces as \(a\leq b\leq c\).

If their sum is already \(7\), Jason rerolls nothing and wins with certainty. Otherwise, if \(a+b\leq6\), he can keep these two dice and reroll the third. Exactly one face completes the sum, giving probability \(1/6\). This exceeds both the largest two-dice reroll probability, \(5/36\), and the three-dice probability, \(5/72\). Thus rerolling two dice is not optimal in these cases.

It remains to consider \(a+b\geq7\). Every pair then sums to at least \(7\), so rerolling one die cannot win. Keeping all three also fails. Rerolling two dice is best exactly when keeping \(a\) beats rerolling all three:
\[
\frac{6-a}{36}>\frac5{72}.
\]
This simplifies to \(a<7/2\), or \(a\leq3\). Equality is impossible for an integer face, so there is no tie between these reroll sizes.

Consequently, the desired initial rolls are precisely those satisfying
\[
a\leq3\qquad\text{and}\qquad a+b\geq7.
\]
Count them using the three distinguishable dice:

| Smallest face | Allowed faces on each other die | Number of ordered rolls |
|---|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(6\) | \(3\cdot1^2=3\) |
| \(2\) | \(5,6\) | \(3\cdot2^2=12\) |
| \(3\) | \(4,5,6\) | \(3\cdot3^2=27\) |

In each row the smallest die is unique, so there are three choices for its position. Each remaining die independently takes any listed face. The rows have different smallest faces, preventing double counting, and the derived conditions show that every qualifying roll is included.

All \(6^3=216\) initial ordered rolls are equally likely. The requested probability is
\[
\frac{3+12+27}{216}
=\frac{42}{216}
=\boxed{\frac7{36}},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
